record.original_question: Can multiscale biological models be analyzed with systematic sensitivity methods that test how higher-level behavior depends on lower-level modeling choices, and can reliable statistical emulators replace prohibitively expensive simulations such as agent-based models without losing the scientifically important behavior being studied?

evidence.quote: Testing the sensitivity to model details, a multiscale modelling equivalent of topological sensitivity analysis, does not seem to be widely used.

Agent-based models can be computationally prohibitively expensive — this is already a problem for parameter estimation for agent-based models. Here there is room for the development of emulation methods that replace expensive simulation by statistical models.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a multiscale biological model in which microscopic-level rules (for example, agent-based dynamics describing individual cells or organisms) give rise to macroscopic emergent behavior (for example, tissue-level patterns or population-level dynamics). Develop a systematic framework that addresses the following two coupled questions:

(1) Multiscale sensitivity analysis. Define and construct a rigorous notion of sensitivity — analogous to topological sensitivity analysis used for single-scale models — that quantifies how features of the higher-level (macroscopic) behavior of the model depend on the structural choices made at the lower (microscopic) level. By "structural choices" we mean not merely numerical parameter values but qualitative modelling decisions such as the form of interaction rules between agents, the choice of stochastic update mechanism, the topology of contact/interaction networks, and the inclusion or exclusion of particular biological mechanisms. The framework should provide quantitative measures of how perturbations of these lower-level modelling choices propagate to changes in the macroscopic observables of interest.

(2) Statistical emulation. For multiscale models whose direct simulation (e.g., large agent-based simulations) is computationally prohibitive, construct statistical emulators — surrogate stochastic models trained on a limited set of simulations — that approximate the input/output map of the full simulator. Establish conditions and methods under which such emulators provably preserve the scientifically relevant qualitative and quantitative features of the macroscopic behavior (for instance, phase transitions, bifurcations, spatial pattern statistics, or long-time population dynamics), together with quantitative error bounds on the discrepancy between emulator predictions and the true simulator output.

Problem: produce such a framework, or prove obstructions to its existence in suitable generality.
artifact.category_tag: multiscale sensitivity and emulation of agent-based models
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a broad methodological program rather than a single conjecture. Surveys and recent work on emulation of agent-based models (e.g., Gaussian-process and neural-network surrogates) and on global/structural sensitivity analysis demonstrate active but partial progress; no general framework for systematic multiscale structural sensitivity coupled with provably reliable emulators has been established. The problem is therefore best classified as open.

status_evidence.title: Open Problems in Mathematical Biology (zbMATH entry)
status_evidence.snippet: Lists multiscale sensitivity analysis and emulation of agent-based models as open methodological challenges in mathematical biology.
status_evidence.claim: The question is posed as an open methodological problem.
